conflicts.point: Whether verifiable compute thresholds effectively isolate frontier risk without imposing prohibitive compliance overhead on open-weight and independent developers.

positions.stance: Tiered compute thresholds effectively target industrial-scale developers while legally exempting open-source repositories and independent researchers from real-time custodian mandates.
Quantitative compute thresholds inevitably impose compliance bleed and legal exposure on mid-sized repositories and open-weight ecosystems, suppressing independent innovation.

conflicts.point: Whether upstream creators of foundational models can maintain or be held accountable for runtime diagnostic interfaces across decentralized downstream deployments.

positions.stance: Upstream developers retain architectural control and responsibility to ensure diagnostic observability without needing permanent runtime custody over local workstations.
Downstream fine-tuning and local execution operate entirely outside the control of upstream model creators, making upstream runtime liability functionally impossible.

verdicts.conflict: Whether verifiable compute thresholds effectively isolate frontier risk without imposing prohibitive compliance overhead on open-weight and independent developers.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist argument prevails on specificity because it identifies exact operational hurdles for mid-sized developers under strict compute rules. The safetyist position lacks equivalent empirical backing to prove that tiered exemptions actually shield independent coders from market exit.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical audits showing that independent developers operating below 10^26 FLOPs face zero legal or financial compliance burdens under tiered safety mandates.

verdicts.conflict: Whether upstream creators of foundational models can maintain or be held accountable for runtime diagnostic interfaces across decentralized downstream deployments.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist position wins on logical validity because upstream developers lose technical control once weights are downloaded and modified locally. The safetyist assumption that upstream entities retain architectural oversight ignores the reality of decentralized fine-tuning.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Technical proof that cryptographic provenance tools or remote diagnostic interfaces can enforce runtime safety compliance on localized open-source hardware without breaking user privacy.
